newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US experts lean toward Sept 24 Fed hike.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US experts lean toward Sept 24 Fed hike.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve will raise short-term interest rates at its policy meeting next week to head off wage-driven inflation, according to a majority of U.S. economists surveyed on Thursday.

Seventeen of 30 economists in the latest Reuters poll said the Federal Reserve is likely to raise short-term interest rates at its Tuesday, September 24 Federal Open Market Committee meeting. All but one of the 17 called for a 25 basis point rate hike.

"There still are wage pressures and some concern the economy is not slowing as fast as the Fed expects," said Dana Saporta, an economist at Stone & McCarthy Research Associates Inc. "I have to concede, though, that it's a very close call."

Of the remaining 13 respondents, seven projected a monetary policy tightening at the November 13 meeting, one called for a rate hike early next year and five said the central bank is on hold for the foreseeable future.
Results were largely unchanged from a September 6 Reuters poll in which 16 of 30 experts called for a rate hike.
As in the previous survey, many prognosticators cited evidence of wage pressures in the August employment report and weekly jobless claims data as reasons for a Fed move.

"Bottom line is the labor market is overheating," said John Williams, chief global markets economist at BT Securities Inc. "(A) 5.1 percent unemployment rate and (low) jobless claims ... tell the tale."
Williams forecast a 25-basis-point boost to the federal funds rate next week.
In August, the unemployment rate dipped to 5.1 percent from 5.4 percent in July as both the average workweek and average hourly earnings grew.
"All of the employment report - not just the unemployment rate - provides a coherent story," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.
Additional evidence of job market tightness recently appeared in anecdotal accounts of labor shortages and the Fed's Beige Book report on regional economic activity, Lieberman said.
"There's nothing that's inconsistent" with the view the Fed will raise rates, he said.

But some economists pointed to last week's inflation data and retail sales figures as evidence to the contrary. Producer and consumer prices grew more slowly than expected in August, and so did retail sales.

"Growth is slowing and inflation remains well-subdued, and with the backdrop of the (Presidential) election it makes sense for (Fed policymakers) to wait until November 13," said Bill Sharp, an economist at Smith Barney Inc.
Sharp predicted a 25-basis-points hike after the election.
Respondents disagreed over how much the election influences Fed policy, but they agreed the campaign was yet another variable to consider ahead of next week's meeting.

"The Fed would like to wait until after the election," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and an economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "(But) there is a definite recognition the Fed could go, and (that) should not be ruled out in its entirety."
